classification.difficultyReason: Reframe the parameterised quartic as a graph comparison, establish an intersection on each side of zero for every k, and justify uniqueness on each side rather than relying on a few representative sketches.

content.prompt: Show that the equation $x^4-kx-1=0$ will always have two real solutions, and that there will always be one positive and one negative solution.

answer.short:
For every real $k$, there are exactly two real solutions, one positive and one negative.

They correspond to the two intersections of $y=x^4-1$ and $y=kx$, one on each side of the $y$-axis.
answer.worked:
Compare $y=x^4-1$ and $y=kx$. At $x=0$, the quartic is below the line; for sufficiently large positive or negative $x$, it is above the line. Continuity gives at least one intersection on each side of the $y$-axis.

To establish that there is only one on each side, note that $x=0$ is not a solution. For $x\ne0$,
$$\begin{align*}x^4-kx-1&=0\\x^3&=k+\frac1x.\end{align*}$$
On each of $x<0$ and $x>0$, $y=x^3$ is strictly increasing, while $y=k+\frac1x$ is strictly decreasing. They can intersect at most once on each interval. Hence the original equation has exactly one negative and one positive solution.
